title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
What Is a Website?
A website is a collection of files that a browser can display. These files usually include:

HTML, which provides the structure
CSS, which controls the appearance
JavaScript, which adds interactivity
Images and other supporting files

My portfolio is made from written source files and then converted into HTML pages by Quarto. GitHub Pages hosts those HTML files so that other people can view them online.
A simple mental model is:

Quarto creates the website, and GitHub Pages publishes it.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
What Is Quarto?
Quarto is a publishing system that converts files written in .qmd format into HTML documents and other outputs such as PDFs, reports, presentations, books, and websites.
A .qmd file combines three things:

YAML, which contains document settings
Markdown, which contains my written content
Code chunks, which run code and display the results

Quarto is useful because it allows writing, coding, analysis, and presentation to exist in the same document.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
How Quarto Works
When I click Render, Quarto processes the .qmd file from top to bottom.
Behind the scenes, it:

Reads the document settings in the YAML section.
Interprets the Markdown text.
Finds the code chunks.
Sends R code to R for evaluation.
Receives the results from R.
Combines my writing, code, and results.
Produces an HTML file.

The result is a finished webpage that can be viewed in a browser.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Anatomy of a .qmd File
A Quarto document usually looks like this:
---
title: "Week 1 Notes"
date: 2026-08-28+
---
This first section is called YAML. It contains metadata and settings for the document.
The body of the document contains Markdown:
## What I Learned

Quarto lets me combine written explanations with executable R code.

[Visit my portfolio](index.qmd)
The document can also contain an R code chunk:

2 + 2

[1] 4


When the document is rendered, the result of the calculation appears underneath the code.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Files and Folders
Different files in the project serve different purposes.

Files for the website

index.qmd is the homepage.
about.qmd is the About page.
weekly-notes/ contains my weekly notes.
assignments/ contains my assignments.



Files for the tools

_quarto.yml contains settings for the entire Quarto website.
freeze/ stores rendered results so that some code does not need to run again.
.Rproj identifies the project as an RStudio project.
.gitignore tells Git which files it should ignore.
.Renviron stores environment variables and private information such as API keys.
docs/ contains the HTML files generated by Quarto for publication.

The files I write are the source files. The files in docs/ are the rendered website.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
How Pages Become Website URLs
The homepage file is usually named index.qmd. When Quarto renders the website, it creates:
docs/index.html
GitHub Pages then displays that file at the main website address.
The same pattern applies to folders:
weekly-notes/index.qmd
        ↓
docs/weekly-notes/index.html
        ↓
myname.github.io/weekly-notes/
The index file acts as the default page for its folder.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Git, GitHub, and GitHub Desktop
These three tools are related, but they are not the same thing.

Git
Git is a version-control system that runs on my computer. It records changes to files and allows me to save labelled snapshots of my work.


GitHub.com
GitHub.com is an online service that stores a copy of my project repository. It also makes the project accessible for collaboration and publishing.


GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop is a graphical interface for Git. It provides buttons for common Git actions.
Two important Git actions are:

Commit: Save a labelled snapshot of changes on my computer.
Push: Send those committed changes to GitHub.com.

After I push changes, GitHub Pages can update the live version of my portfolio.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
R Scripts and Quarto Documents
An R script contains mainly R code:
x <- 10
x + 5
A Quarto document is more flexible. It can contain:

Written explanations
Headings
Links
Images
R code
Tables
Charts
Code results

This makes Quarto useful for documenting not only what I calculated, but also why I calculated it and what the results mean.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
My Mental Model
I now think of my portfolio as having three versions:

My computer: where I edit the source files
GitHub.com: where Git stores and tracks the project
My live website: what visitors see in their browser

The complete process is:
Write or edit a .qmd file
        ↓
Render it with Quarto
        ↓
Review the generated HTML
        ↓
Commit the changes with Git
        ↓
Push the commit to GitHub
        ↓
GitHub Pages updates the website

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
RStudio, Scripts, and Code Chunks
There are several ways to write and run R code.

The Console
The R Console runs code immediately and displays the result:
2 + 2
The Console is useful for quick experiments. However, code entered there is temporary in the sense that it is not automatically saved as part of a reproducible analysis. The objects remain in the current R session, but they can disappear when the session is restarted.


R Scripts
An R script contains R code saved in a file with the .R extension:
result <- 2 + 2
Scripts are useful for saving and rerunning code.


Quarto Code Chunks
A Quarto document can contain written explanations and executable R code:

2 + 2

[1] 4


When the document is rendered, the code runs and its result appears in the final webpage.
A useful mental model is:

The Console is for experimentation.
An R script is for saving code.
A Quarto document is for combining code, explanation, and results.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Packages
An R package is a collection of functions and data that extends what R can do.
You usually install a package once:
install.packages("dplyr")
Installing a package is like buying a book. You normally do not need to buy the same book every time you want to read it.
Before using a package in a new R session, load it:
library(dplyr)
Loading a package is like taking the book off the shelf so that you can use it.
For example:
library(tidycensus)
You generally load the package each time you start a new R session and want to use it.
The correct spelling is:
library(dplyr)
not:
library(deplyr)

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Tibbles and Data Frames
A tibble is a modern version of an R data frame. Both store data in rows and columns, but tibbles print more clearly and provide more information when displayed.
For example:
county_data
A tibble usually shows:

The column names
The data types
A limited number of rows
The number of observations and variables

A tibble is not a verb. It is a type of data object.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
R Is Case-Sensitive
R treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.
These are different names:
select()
Select()
The correct tidyverse function is:
select()
This also applies to object and column names:
moe_pct
MOE_PCT
These are not the same column name.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Common Data-Verbs
The tidyverse provides functions that work like verbs. Each function performs a common data operation.

filter() Selects Rows
filter() keeps rows that meet a condition.
large_counties <- filter(
  counties,
  population > 5000
)
This keeps counties whose population is greater than 5,000.
A helpful way to remember it is:

filter() chooses observations.



select() Selects Columns
select() keeps particular columns.
county_subset <- select(
  counties,
  NAME,
  population
)
This keeps only the NAME and population columns.
A helpful way to remember it is:

select() chooses variables.



mutate() Creates or Modifies Columns
mutate() creates a new column or changes an existing column.
new_counties <- mutate(
  counties,
  income_thousands = income / 1000
)
This creates a new column called income_thousands.
The general pattern is:
new_data <- mutate(
  old_data,
  new_column = calculation
)


arrange() Changes Row Order
arrange() sorts rows.
arrange(counties, population)
This sorts from smallest to largest population.
To sort from largest to smallest, use desc():
arrange(counties, desc(population))
The function is lowercase:
arrange()
not:
Arrange()


group_by() Defines Groups
group_by() tells R to treat observations as belonging to groups.
counties %>%
  group_by(state)
This does not summarize the data by itself. It prepares the data for a grouped operation.


summarize() Reduces Groups
summarize() calculates summary values for each group.
Suppose the data looks like this:



County
State
Income




Orange
NY
70,000


Nassau
NY
80,000


Sacramento
CA
100,000


Orange
NY
90,000



We can calculate the minimum income for each state:
counties %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(
    min_income = min(income)
  )
The result would be:



State
Minimum income




NY
70,000


CA
100,000



group_by() defines the groups, while summarize() calculates the result for each group.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Pipes
Without pipes, a multi-step workflow may require several intermediate objects:
step1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)

step2 <- arrange(step1, desc(moe_pct))

step3 <- select(step2, NAME, moe_pct)
Pipes allow these steps to be connected:
new_data <- counties %>%
  filter(moe_pct > 10) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
The pipe passes the result from one function into the next.
In plain language, this means:

Start with counties.
Keep counties where moe_pct is greater than 10.
Sort them from largest to smallest moe_pct.
Keep only NAME and moe_pct.

R also has a newer native pipe:
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
Both %>% and |> are used to build readable workflows.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
section: The U.S. Census and the ACS
text:
The U.S. Census and the ACS
The U.S. Constitution requires a population count every ten years. This is called the Decennial Census.
The Decennial Census counts people living in the United States, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Its main purpose is to produce a complete population count and support political representation and resource allocation.
The American Community Survey, or ACS, is different. It is an ongoing sample survey that collects information about topics such as:

Income
Education
Employment
Housing
Disability
Race and ethnicity
Transportation
Health-related characteristics

The ACS uses a sample of households to estimate characteristics for the wider population.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
ACS Products

ACS 1-Year Estimates
ACS 1-year estimates are generally available for larger populations and places. They provide more recent estimates but may not be available for smaller areas.


ACS 3-Year Estimates
The ACS 3-year estimates were discontinued after the 2013 data release.


ACS 5-Year Estimates
ACS 5-year estimates combine five years of survey data. They are available for smaller populations and smaller geographies, including census tracts and, for many variables, block groups.
For example, a 2023 ACS 5-year estimate generally represents data collected during:
2019–2023
It is not a single-year estimate. It summarizes information collected across the five-year period.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Estimates and Margins of Error
ACS results include an estimate and a margin of error.
For example:
Estimate = 38.7
Margin of error = 0.2
This can be written as:
38.7 ± 0.2
The estimate is the reported value, while the margin of error describes the uncertainty around that estimate.
Smaller places often have smaller samples. Because fewer households are surveyed, estimates for small places can have larger margins of error.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Census Variable Codes
Census variables have codes that identify the table, line, and type of value.
For example:
B19013_001E
The code can be understood as:

B = base table
19013 = table number
001 = line number
E = estimate

The margin-of-error version uses M:
B19013_001M
In many tidycensus functions, the estimate variable can be requested without the final E:
"B19013_001"
However, the full Census variable code is often shown as:
B19013_001E

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Finding Census Variables
The load_variables() function retrieves the Census variable dictionary.
library(tidycensus)

variables <- load_variables(
  year = 2023,
  dataset = "acs5"
)
This gives information about available variables, including:

Variable codes
Variable labels
Table names
Concepts

load_variables() helps identify and understand variables. It does not download the actual county data.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Downloading ACS Data
The get_acs() function downloads ACS data.
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    "B19013_001",
    "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
This requests two variables for Pennsylvania counties using the 2023 ACS 5-year survey.
The result is usually returned in tidy, long format.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Census Geographies
A census tract is a statistical area designed to represent a relatively small community. A tract usually contains approximately 1,200 to 8,000 people, with an ideal population of about 4,000.
A tract can be used as a rough geographic proxy for a neighborhood, although a tract is not always the same as a socially recognized neighborhood.
Census tracts are generally revised during the decennial Census. Their boundaries can change, which makes comparisons across years more difficult.
To compare geography consistently over time, researchers sometimes use harmonized geography products such as:

NHGIS
LTDB

These products provide tools or crosswalks for comparing geographic areas across different boundary systems.
Block groups are smaller than census tracts. Because they contain fewer people, their estimates can have larger margins of error.
A census block is the smallest Census geography. Blocks are used in the Decennial Census but generally do not have the same level of ACS data available as larger geographies.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
GEOIDs
A GEOID is a unique identifier for a Census geography.
A county GEOID contains five digits:
Two-digit state code + three-digit county code
A census tract GEOID contains eleven digits:
Two-digit state code
+ three-digit county code
+ six-digit tract code
A block-group GEOID contains twelve digits:
Census tract GEOID + one-digit block-group code
GEOIDs should usually be stored as character strings rather than numbers.
For example:
06001
If this value is stored as a number, R may remove the leading zero:
6001
That can cause problems when joining Census data to geographic boundary data.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Long and Wide Data
By default, get_acs() returns data in long format.
In long format, each geography-variable combination usually occupies its own row. This is useful when working with one variable at a time or creating maps.
Wide format places multiple variables in separate columns. This is often more convenient when comparing variables or calculating relationships between them.
To request wide data directly:
county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    myvar = "B01002_001",
    pop = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "CA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)
Because the variables were named myvar and pop, the resulting columns will include:
myvarE
myvarM
popE
popM
The suffixes mean:

E = estimate
M = margin of error

For example:
county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(
    moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100
  )
This calculates the margin of error as a percentage of the estimate.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
A Complete Data Workflow
A typical workflow might look like this:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B01002_001",
  state = "CA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct)

head(county_data, 10)
This workflow:

Downloads county-level ACS data.
Calculates the relative margin of error.
Sorts counties from highest to lowest relative margin of error.
Keeps only the relevant columns.
Displays the ten counties with the largest relative margins of error.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Lessons
This week, I learned that R analysis is often built as a sequence of small transformations. Each function performs one task, and pipes allow those tasks to be connected into a readable workflow.
I also learned that Census data requires attention to geography, time period, variable definitions, estimates, and margins of error. A reported estimate should not automatically be treated as equally reliable across all places. Smaller geographies often have smaller samples and greater uncertainty.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Use library(dplyr), not library(deplyr).
R functions are case-sensitive, so use select() and arrange().
Close every pipe and parenthesis correctly.
Make sure column names match exactly.
Store GEOIDs as character strings.
Remember that ACS 5-year estimates cover five years of data.
Do not confuse an estimate with its margin of error.
Use load_variables() to understand variables and get_acs() to download data.
Use output = "wide" when comparing multiple variables side by side.

title: About Me
text:
I am a Ghanaian geospatial scientist and GIS team lead with a background in Geospatial Engineering. Before joining Penn’s Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program, I worked at Zipline International in Kigali, where I helped develop geospatial systems for autonomous medical drone delivery. This work involved terrain modeling, aerial imagery, route planning, and spatial data management across complex environments. It showed me how geospatial technology can have a direct human impact, from helping patients receive medical supplies on time to improving access to essential services.
My interest in urban spatial analytics grew from seeing how invisible or incomplete spatial data can limit effective planning. Earlier in my career, I worked on mapping underserved communities and sanitation infrastructure, producing information that helped support improved sanitation for more than 3,000 communities. These experiences taught me that maps are not just technical products. They influence how resources are allocated, which communities receive attention, and how governments and organizations respond to urgent needs.
At MUSA, I am strengthening my skills in statistics, programming, spatial modeling, data visualization, and urban systems. I am particularly interested in routing, mapping, geospatial software, and the spatial intelligence that supports technologies such as delivery platforms, autonomous vehicles, and self-driving systems. I hope to work with technology companies developing products that depend on accurate maps, efficient routing, and a strong understanding of the built environment.
Across these interests, my central goal is to help create a more equitable society. Whether I am working on public infrastructure, medical delivery, transportation, or autonomous technology, I want to contribute to systems that are more accessible, reliable, and responsive to the needs of underserved communities.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?

Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "CA"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B01002_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Alpine County, California        41.1   4.8   11.7 
 2 Sierra County, California        56     5      8.93
 3 Mono County, California          40.3   1.8    4.47

Alpine County is the least reliable county in the dataset, with the highest relative margin of error(moe_pct) at approximately 11.68%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4  ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    42
2 Low confidence      4
3 Moderate           12


Using the original thresholds, 56 counties were classified as high confidence, 1 as moderate, and 1 as low confidence. Because this classification was highly concentrated in one category, I adjusted the thresholds to 1% and 4% to make differences in relative margin of error more informative for this county-level dataset.

text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The least reliable estimates came from Alpine, Sierra, Mono, and Modoc Counties. Their average population was 6,560, compared with 924,758 for the 42 high-confidence counties.
This happens because the ACS uses a sample of households. Smaller counties have fewer households in the sample, so their estimates have more uncertainty and larger margins of error.
If a state agency treated every estimate as equally reliable, these rural counties could receive less funding than they need for healthcare, transportation, housing, or services for older residents. Funding decisions should account for both the estimate and its margin of error.

My Reflections
This week helped me understand how R can be used to move from raw data to a clear result. Using pipes also made the code easier to follow because I could connect several steps without creating a new object after every operation.
I also learned how to use tidycensus to download American Community Survey data. Before this, I mostly thought of Census data as a table of numbers. Working with estimates and margins of error showed me that the numbers also have different levels of reliability. The exercise also showed me why it is important to understand the structure of the data before analyzing it. section: Joining Tables: Match by an Identifier
text:
Joining Tables: Match by an Identifier
A join combines information from two tables using a shared key. For Census tables, the key is often GEOID.

The example from class
These are small invented tables to make the joins easy to follow. The three-digit identifiers are teaching examples, not real tract GEOIDs.

income_23_example <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "300"),
  med_inc_23 = c(82000, 31500, 45000)
)

income_15_example <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "400"),
  med_inc_15 = c(61000, 27000, 39000)
)

income_23_example

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  GEOID med_inc_23
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 100        82000
2 200        31500
3 300        45000

income_15_example

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  GEOID med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 100        61000
2 200        27000
3 400        39000



left_join(income_23_example, income_15_example, by = "GEOID")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000
3 300        45000         NA


The result is:

med_inc_15

The third identifier stays 300 because it came from the left table. It does not become 400. There is no 2015 match for 300, so its new income column contains NA. The 2015-only row for 400 is excluded.
Read left_join(x, y, by = "GEOID") as: keep the rows from x, find matching keys in y, and bring over their columns.


Reading the Venn diagram
The photograph from class illustrates table joins. Think of the circles as sets of identifiers. The shaded left circle includes identifiers with and without a match; the shared middle contains identifiers found in both tables; both circles together contain all identifiers.

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15

1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000
3 300        45000         NA

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  GEOID med_inc_23
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 300        45000


The circles are a memory aid, but real joins match rows, not just sets. If a key appears twice in the right table, one matching left row can become two output rows. A left join retains every left row, but it does not always retain the original row count. Swapping the inputs of a left join keeps the other table’s rows, which is why we often use a left join instead of switching to a right join. dplyr join reference


Why GEOIDs should be text
A tract GEOID has 11 characters: 2 for the state + 3 for the county + 6 for the tract. The tract part is six characters, not four. A block-group GEOID adds one more character. Census GEOID guide

example_geoid <- "06001400100"
nchar(example_geoid)

[1] 11

as.numeric(example_geoid)

[1] 6001400100


The numeric conversion drops the leading zero. A GEOID identifies a place; it is not a quantity to calculate with. Store it as character text and use compatible key types on both sides of a join. Changing a damaged number back with as.character() does not restore a missing zero automatically.
R is case-sensitive: GEOID, Geoid, and geoid are different names. Function names are also case-sensitive: use left_join(), not Left_join().

section: Spatial Data: A Table Plus Geometry
text:
Spatial Data: A Table Plus Geometry
An sf object is a data frame with a special geometry column and spatial metadata. It can hold points, lines, polygons, or their multi-feature versions. The geometry records the coordinates; the other columns hold attributes such as income or population.

A bike-share station can be a POINT.
A street can be a LINESTRING.
A tract can be a POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON.

A polygon needs a closed boundary made from several coordinates. A single coordinate pair is a point, not a complete polygon.
sf stands for simple features. It is an R package and an object representation. Shapefiles, GeoJSON, and GeoPackages are storage formats that sf can read or write; they are not the same thing as an sf object. Introduction to sf
Three related names appear in R: sf is the complete spatial table, sfc is its geometry list-column, and sfg represents one geometry. st_geometry(x) extracts the geometry, while st_drop_geometry(x) gives us the attributes without geometry. These are different operations.

Pull ACS data with boundaries

tract_file <- file.path(data_dir, "philly-tracts-acs2023.rds")

} else {

    state = "PA",

    variables = c(

      total_pop = "B01003_001"

    year = 2023,

section: Income Reliability and Our First Map
text:
Income Reliability and Our First Map
We retain tracts with a positive population estimate, as in the lab. We also keep the original unfiltered object for checking joins later.

philly_tracts <- tracts_2023_all %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    med_inc_se = if_else(
      !is.na(med_incM) & med_incM >= 0,
      med_incM / 1.645,
      NA_real_
    ),
    med_inc_cv = if_else(
      !is.na(med_incE) & med_incE > 0,
      med_inc_se / med_incE * 100,
      NA_real_
    ),
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(med_inc_cv) ~ "Unavailable",
      med_inc_cv < 12 ~ "High",
      med_inc_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE ~ "Low"
    )
  )

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(reliability)

  reliability   n
1        High 104
2         Low  23
3    Moderate 254
4 Unavailable  10


The ACS MOE is normally reported at the 90% confidence level, so we use the conversion in the Census accuracy worked examples:
[ SE = MOE / 1.645, CV = (SE / estimate). ]
These are the lab’s CV categories: below 12%, 12% through 40%, and above 40%. They are not the Week 2 categories based on moe_pct. CV and relative MOE differ by the factor 1.645. The labels summarize relative sampling uncertainty; they do not turn an estimate into a certainty.
The missing-value rule comes first so an unavailable CV does not fall through to “Low.” An undefined income estimate is not a zero-dollar income. Income with an invalid or unavailable MOE also cannot receive a numeric CV here.

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    retained_tracts = n(),
    missing_income = sum(is.na(med_incE)),
    unavailable_cv = sum(is.na(med_inc_cv))

Why a successful join is not enough for change over time
Tracts can split, merge, or change boundaries between Census geography vintages. The 2015 and 2023 ACS products straddle the 2020 tract revisions. A missing match is a reason to investigate; even a matching GEOID does not prove that the geographic footprint stayed identical.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems
A coordinate reference system, or CRS, explains what coordinates mean: their reference framework, axes, units, and, where applicable, projection. Numbers alone do not tell us whether a point is in Philadelphia, whether its units are feet, or whether its coordinates are longitude and latitude.

The geoid, ellipsoid, and datum
The recording includes the background behind these terms:

The geoid is a gravity-based reference surface approximating mean sea level, extended under the continents. It is not a model of every mountain and valley.
An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical Earth model, slightly flattened at the poles. It gives us a manageable surface for coordinates.
A geodetic datum or reference frame connects that model and its coordinates to locations on Earth.
A geographic CRS adds a coordinate system, axes, and angular units to that reference framework. A datum alone is not the entire CRS.

The lowercase geoid in this discussion is completely different from the Census GEOID identifier. One is a reference surface; the other is a code in our data table. NOAA’s geoid explanation
The historical example from class was NAD27: it uses the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and a reference origin at Meades Ranch, Kansas. NAD83 uses GRS80 and was developed with a geocentric reference framework. The same numeric longitude and latitude can therefore refer to different ground positions under different datums. WGS84 is another widely used global reference system associated with GPS. NOAA’s datum FAQ
The practical lesson is to inspect the full CRS, not just check whether both layers use degrees. A datum mismatch can create a location offset even when two layers look almost aligned. The size of that offset depends on the systems and location; there is no universal correction to add by hand.

Easting and northing
Often meters or feet
Planar coordinates designed for a region or purpose



A degree of longitude does not have the same ground length at every latitude. A buffer distance of 0.5 is therefore not automatically half a mile. For this lab, a local projected CRS makes distances and areas easier to interpret.
Geographic coordinates can still support geodesic distance calculations with appropriate software. The point is to understand the calculation and units, not to assume every operation in longitude and latitude is invalid.
In the common signed decimal-degree convention, longitude runs from -180 to 180 and latitude from -90 to 90. A Philadelphia coordinate near longitude -75 and latitude 40 is plausible. Those ranges are useful clues, not proof of a CRS. Confirm the metadata. In typical sf point construction, x is longitude and y is latitude when supplying longitude/latitude coordinates.


Projections preserve different properties
Common projection families include cylindrical, transverse cylindrical, conic, and azimuthal (planar). These describe how a projection is constructed. A separate question is what it preserves.
The class demonstration used an orange and a sheet of paper to explain flattening a curved surface. It is a useful analogy for distortion, although many projections are mathematical transformations rather than literal shadows from a light. Tangent and secant constructions help explain reference lines or points where scale is controlled. A projection works best in its intended region, not equally well everywhere.








Property
Meaning
Caution




Conformal
Preserves local angles and shapes at very small scales
Does not preserve area; Lambert Conformal Conic is an example


Equal-area
Preserves area relationships
Useful when area comparison matters; shapes can be distorted


Equidistant
Preserves specified distances, such as from a chosen center
Does not preserve every distance everywhere


Direction
Some projections preserve bearings from a chosen center
No flat map preserves every direction, area, and distance globally



Mercator is conformal and shows constant-bearing routes, or rhumb lines, as straight lines. That does not mean every straight line is the shortest route, or that all distances and directions between arbitrary points are preserved.


CRS codes used in class









EPSG
CRS
Units
Useful context




2272
NAD83 / Pennsylvania South (ftUS)
US survey feet
Local analysis around Philadelphia


5070
NAD83 / Conus Albers
Meters
Equal-area work across the contiguous United States


4326
WGS 84
Degrees
Common geographic coordinates


4269
NAD83
Degrees
Common in US geographic datasets


26918
NAD83 / UTM zone 18N
Meters
A projected option for Philadelphia



EPSG 2272 is specifically the US survey-foot version. It is not “feet or meters” interchangeably. A meter-based State Plane definition uses a different CRS code.
UTM divides the world into 60 numbered longitudinal zones, with northern and southern hemisphere versions. Zone numbers run from 1 to 60; there are no negative zone numbers. The hemisphere and datum matter as well as the zone. Large easting and northing values are normal and do not mean the coordinates are wrong.


Inspect, transform, or label?







Function
What it does




st_crs(x)
Reads the object’s CRS metadata


st_transform(x, 2272)
Converts coordinates from their known source CRS to the target CRS


st_set_crs(x, 4326)
Assigns or replaces a CRS label without moving the coordinates



The normal workflow is check the CRS, then transform if needed. There is no extra st_set_crs() step after st_transform().
The recording’s jar analogy helps: putting a “salt” label on a jar of sugar does not change what is inside. Likewise, calling st_set_crs(x, 2272) on longitude/latitude numbers does not convert them into feet. It only gives those same numbers a different interpretation. st_transform() performs the coordinate conversion and updates the label together.
Only use st_set_crs() when reliable information establishes what the existing coordinates already mean. Assigning a label to unknown coordinates by guesswork can place the data in the wrong location. sf transformation reference

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Spatial Operations: Match by Location
Table joins ask whether keys match. Spatial operations ask whether geometries have a relationship, such as intersecting, touching, containing, or being within a specified distance.

Predicates answer a relationship question







Function
Relationship tested




st_intersects(x, y)
The features share any point, including a boundary point


st_touches(x, y)
The boundaries meet, but the interiors do not intersect


st_within(x, y)
Each feature in x lies within a feature in y, according to the predicate’s boundary rules


st_contains(x, y)
The corresponding containment question with the roles reversed


st_disjoint(x, y)
The features share no points


st_is_within_distance(x, y, dist = ...)
Their minimum distance is within the supplied distance



st_touches() is more specific than everyday “touches.” A tract overlapping the inside of a station buffer intersects it; it usually does not satisfy st_touches(). Use st_intersects() when “any overlap or contact” is the intended rule. sf spatial predicates
For the classroom polygon example, imagine polygon B beside A with a shared edge, C entirely inside A, and D separated from A:



Relationship to A
Intersects A?
Touches A?
Within A?




B shares an edge, with no interior overlap
TRUE
TRUE
FALSE


C is entirely inside A, away from its boundary
TRUE
FALSE
TRUE


D is separated from A
FALSE
FALSE
FALSE



“Intersects” is the broad test. It includes containment as well as boundary contact and partial overlap. “Touches” excludes interior overlap.
The default result of many predicates is a sparse list of matching row positions. For example, the first element of st_intersects(tracts, stations) tells us which station rows intersect the first tract. lengths() counts matches for every element of that list. The singular length() would count the list’s elements, usually the number of input tracts.


Filter, join, or change the shapes?








Operation
Result
Does it cut the original shapes?




st_filter(x, y)
Selected whole features from x
No


st_join(x, y)
Features of x with matched attributes from y
No; rows may repeat for multiple matches


st_intersection(x, y)
Shared geometric portions
Yes


st_difference(x, y)
Portions of x outside y
Yes


st_sym_difference(x, y)
Portions belonging to one side but not both
Yes


st_union(x)
Combined geometry with internal overlap dissolved
Merges shapes


st_distance(x, y)
Distances between features
Returns measurements, not a new polygon layer



st_union() combines geometric coverage; it does not automatically add population or compute an income statistic. Likewise, st_intersection() can copy attributes to fragments, but it does not automatically estimate how many residents live in each fragment. sf geometry operations
Names can differ in meaning across GIS software. In this lab, the one-input st_union(x) dissolves the geometries together. Do not assume it produces the same attribute-preserving polygon subdivision as a desktop GIS tool named “Union.”


A spatial version of the overlapping-circle picture
Unlike the table-join diagram, this picture shows actual areas being combined or cut. The circles below are synthetic teaching shapes, not Indego results.

circle_a <- st_sfc(st_point(c(2600000, 240000)), crs = 2272) %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 800)
circle_b <- st_sfc(st_point(c(2601000, 240000)), crs = 2272) %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 800)

original_circles <- st_sf(geometry = c(circle_a, circle_b))

operation_shapes <- st_sf(
  operation = factor(
    c("Intersection: shared area", "Union: either circle",
      "Difference: A outside B", "Symmetric difference: one only"),
    levels = c("Intersection: shared area", "Union: either circle",
               "Difference: A outside B", "Symmetric difference: one only")
  ),
  geometry = c(
    st_intersection(circle_a, circle_b),
    st_union(c(circle_a, circle_b)),
    st_difference(circle_a, circle_b),
    st_sym_difference(circle_a, circle_b)
  )
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = operation_shapes, fill = "#2A9D8F", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = original_circles, fill = NA, color = "grey35") +
  facet_wrap(~operation, ncol = 2) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()




Colored regions are the output of each operation. The gray outlines show the two original circles.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Distance to the Nearest Station

A tract needs a representative point

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

We use each tract’s geometric centroid as a simple starting location. A centroid is not necessarily where most residents live, and it can fall outside an irregular polygon. st_point_on_surface() gives a point inside the polygon, but that point is not automatically a population center either.


All pairs versus one pair per tract

distance_matrix <- st_distance(centroids, stations)
dim(distance_matrix)

[1] 391 319

distance_matrix[
  seq_len(min(3, nrow(distance_matrix))),
  seq_len(min(3, ncol(distance_matrix))),
  drop = FALSE
]

Units: [US_survey_foot]
         [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
[1,] 4533.641 4669.516 12892.29
[2,] 5180.532 5051.223 13057.11
[3,] 9107.896 8324.892 14469.92


The rows represent tract centroids and the columns represent stations. Each cell is the distance for that pair. These measurements carry units. Without by_element = TRUE, this is a full matrix, not one distance per tract. Large all-pairs matrices can be expensive, so the next approach is more useful when we only need the nearest station. sf distance measurements
The geometries I pass in change the question. st_distance(philly_tracts, stations) measures the minimum distance between each polygon and each station, so a station inside a tract has distance zero from that tract. Using centroids instead measures from its representative point. Distance to a tract’s boundary or footprint and distance from its centroid are not interchangeable.

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, stations)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    nearest_station = stations$name[nearest_idx],
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(
        centroids,
        stations[nearest_idx, ],
        by_element = TRUE
      )
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / 5280
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
 0.01893  0.15554  0.41382  1.84137  2.73916 10.93093 


nearest_idx contains station row positions, not distances. stations[nearest_idx, ] selects one matching station per tract, in tract order. by_element = TRUE then compares the first centroid with the first selected station, the second with the second, and so on.
If I were sorting distances manually, the nearest would be the smallest distance: ascending order. arrange(desc(distance)) would put the farthest first. st_nearest_feature() avoids building and sorting a full distance table for this task.
as.numeric() removes the units label after we have checked that the CRS uses feet. Dividing by 5,280 expresses the distance in the lab’s miles. These are straight-line distances, not walking routes. Rivers, rail yards, highways, entrances, and bridges can make a short straight-line distance a much longer journey.

ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dist_mi), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = stations, inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 0.5, color = "white") +

section: Half-Mile Buffers: Filter Whole Tracts or Cut Their Shapes
text:
Half-Mile Buffers: Filter Whole Tracts or Cut Their Shapes
A buffer creates an area within a specified distance of a feature. Here each station gets a 2,640-foot circle. Unioning the buffers combines overlapping circles so shared areas are not counted repeatedly.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = philly_tracts, fill = "grey95", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = station_zone, fill = "#56B4E9", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = stations, size = 0.4) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Half-mile zones around Indego stations",
    subtitle = "Overlapping station buffers have been dissolved into one geometry"
  )








The union can contain separated pieces in a MULTIPOLYGON. “One geometry” does not mean every station circle connects to every other one. sf buffers and other unary operations

st_filter(): keep the whole tract

tracts_near_stations <- st_filter(philly_tracts, station_zone)

outside_zone <- st_filter(
  philly_tracts,
  station_zone,
  .predicate = st_disjoint
)

tibble(
  relationship = c("Any intersection with zone", "No intersection with zone"),
  n_tracts = c(nrow(tracts_near_stations), nrow(outside_zone))
)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  relationship               n_tracts
  <chr>                         <int>
1 Any intersection with zone      229
2 No intersection with zone       162


The default filter predicate is st_intersects(). A tract with even a tiny overlap, or just a shared boundary point, is selected whole. Its geometry is not trimmed to the buffer.
If the question instead asks for tracts entirely within the zone, make that predicate explicit:

entirely_within_zone <- st_filter(
  philly_tracts,
  station_zone,
  .predicate = st_within
)
nrow(entirely_within_zone)

[1] 169


st_filter() returns selected features. nrow() counts them. The function does not return a count by itself, and it does not require full containment unless we choose that relationship.
We use the unioned station zone for the disjoint test. Filtering for disjointness against individual station buffers could retain a tract simply because it is far from one station, even if it is beside another.


st_intersection(): keep only the covered portion

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  select(GEOID) %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  summarize(covered_area = sum(covered_area), .groups = "drop")

Warning: attribute variables are assumed to be spatially constant throughout
all geometries

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(
    covered_area = replace_na(covered_area, 0),
    pct_covered = if_else(
      tract_area > 0,
      100 * covered_area / tract_area,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(philly_tracts$GEOID))
summary(philly_tracts$pct_covered)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00    0.00   71.73   52.05  100.00  100.00 


The steps are:

Measure each original tract’s area.
Cut the tract at the station-zone boundary.
Measure the retained portion and sum any fragments for that GEOID.
Drop geometry from the coverage table.
Join the measurements back to the original whole tracts.
Divide covered area by original area and multiply by 100.

Both areas use the same squared units, so the units cancel in the percentage. A tract with no intersecting portion has zero covered area. We join only one coverage record per GEOID to prevent duplicated tract rows.
We select only GEOID before the intersection because we need a spatial measurement, not copied income estimates on each fragment. An income estimate does not become an estimate for the clipped fragment just because its polygon was cut.
Some sf versions print a warning that attributes are assumed to be spatially constant when performing an overlay. Here the retained attribute is just the tract identifier. We are measuring clipped geometry, not assuming that income or population is evenly distributed inside the tract.

ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pct_covered), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    labels = function(x) paste0(round(x), "%"),
    na.value = "grey80"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Tract area within half a mile of an Indego station",
    subtitle = "Area coverage is not the percentage of residents served",
    fill = "Area covered"
  )








A tract could be half covered by area while most homes are in its uncovered half. Water, industrial land, parks, and uneven settlement matter. This is an area-based indicator, not a direct resident-access rate.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: Worked Challenge: Which Low-Income Tracts Lack Access?
text:
Worked Challenge: Which Low-Income Tracts Lack Access?
For this example:

Low income: a tract’s 2019–2023 median household income is at or below the 25th percentile among populated Philadelphia tracts with a known positive estimate.
Access: the tract centroid is within half a mile of its nearest station.

This is a relative citywide income definition, not an official poverty threshold. Ties at the cutoff can put slightly more than 25% of eligible tracts in the group. Missing income stays unknown and is not treated as high income.

known_income <- philly_tracts$med_incE[
  !is.na(philly_tracts$med_incE) & philly_tracts$med_incE > 0
]
stopifnot(length(known_income) > 0)

income_cutoff <- unname(quantile(known_income, probs = 0.25))

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    low_income = case_when(
      is.na(med_incE) | med_incE <= 0 ~ NA,
      TRUE ~ med_incE <= income_cutoff
    ),
    access_centroid = dist_mi <= 0.5,
    access_any_overlap = lengths(st_intersects(., station_zone)) > 0,
    access_half_area = pct_covered >= 50
  )

Each row uses the same low-income group and station snapshot. Only the access rule changes. The any-overlap rule can classify a tract as served when the station zone covers just a small corner. The 50%-area rule demands more coverage but still makes no claim about where residents live. The centroid rule is easy to explain but reduces an entire tract to one point.
A possible defense of the worked choice is: I used centroid distance as a first screening measure because it gives each tract a comparable distance to its nearest station. It does not describe every resident’s journey, so I also compared overlap and area coverage to see how much the result depends on that choice.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: What We Can and Cannot Conclude
text:
What We Can and Cannot Conclude

Income: a tract median describes households collectively. It does not establish that every resident is low-income.
Sampling uncertainty: CV and MOE help describe uncertainty in the ACS estimate. They do not account for every possible source of error.
Location: an intersecting station, a nearby centroid, and a large covered area measure different things.
Travel: straight-line proximity does not measure walking time, safe crossings, or cycling conditions.
Service: a station point does not guarantee available bikes, available docks, affordable membership, or reliable service. The feed’s totalDocks field, if present, could support a separate capacity question.
Time: the station snapshot is contemporary to its download; the ACS estimates describe 2019–2023. This is not a reconstruction of 2023 service unless we obtain historical station data.
Boundaries: joining records is not the same as making different geography vintages comparable.

These checks help distinguish a useful screening map from a stronger claim about who Indego actually serves.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
My Mental Model
I start with a question, then decide what one row and one place represent. I check identifiers before a table join and coordinate systems before a spatial operation. I use a predicate to test a relationship, a filter to keep whole features, an overlay to create new shapes, and a join to attach attributes.
The biggest lesson from the lab is that “access” needs a definition. A map can look precise while hiding choices about boundaries, distance, population, and uncertainty. I need to state those choices so another person can understand what the result actually measures.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
This week connected data visualization with uncertainty in American Community Survey estimates. We practiced using ggplot2, calculating margins of error for derived values, comparing ACS estimates across time, and creating reusable R functions.
The examples use New York county data and the 2023 ACS 5-year survey. The charts are included in the rendered page, while the code is hidden.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Setup
Install these packages once in the R console, not inside this document:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidycensus", "gt"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(gt)

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
The Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 creates plots by mapping variables in a data frame to visual properties.



Data variable
Plot feature




Estimate
Position on an axis


Population
Position on an axis


Reliability
Color


Margin of error
Size or error bars



This approach is called the Grammar of Graphics. A plot is built from separate parts that work together.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Creating ACS Data
B17001_002 represents the number of people below 100% of the poverty level.

my_variable <- "B17001_002"
my_state <- "NY"

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Important columns include:

GEOID: geographic identifier
NAME: county name
estimate: Census estimate
moe: margin of error

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Relative Margin of Error
To compare uncertainty across counties, calculate the margin of error as a percentage of the estimate:

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

A relative margin of error is useful because the same absolute MOE can have different meanings for different-sized estimates.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Reliability Categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    reliability = case_when(
      moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
      moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )

case_when() checks conditions from top to bottom. The first condition that is TRUE determines the category. The final TRUE catches all remaining values.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Basic Scatterplot
A basic ggplot2 plot contains the data, aesthetic mappings, and a geometric object.

ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point()








The first argument must be the name of an actual data frame. For example, ggplot(data, ...) would be incorrect here because data is only a placeholder.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Mapping Versus Decorating
When a visual property depends on a variable, put it inside aes():

ggplot(county_data, aes(
  x = estimate,
  y = moe_pct,
  color = reliability
)) +
  geom_point()








When every point should have the same color, put the color outside aes():

ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")








aes(color = reliability)       # maps a variable
geom_point(color = "blue")     # sets one fixed color

text:
Common Geometries



Question
Useful geometry




How is one variable distributed?
geom_histogram()


How are two variables related?
geom_point()


How do groups compare?
geom_boxplot() or geom_col()


How does something change over time?
geom_line()


How uncertain is an estimate?
geom_errorbar()

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Error Bars
An error bar shows the estimate together with its margin of error:

county_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = estimate - moe,
      ymax = estimate + moe
    )
  )








The first aes() supplies mappings shared by the layers. The second aes() supplies the ymin and ymax mappings needed specifically by geom_errorbar().
The full chart is difficult to read, so we can keep the 15 counties with the largest relative margins of error:

top_15 <- county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York"))

ggplot(top_15, aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Counties with the Largest Margins of Error",
    subtitle = "People below 100% of the poverty level, ACS 2023 5-year estimates",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Population below poverty level"
  )

text:
Facets and Themes
A facet creates a separate panel for each category:

ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~reliability) +
  theme_minimal()








Themes change the appearance of a plot without changing the data.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Derived Uncertainty
When we calculate a new value from Census estimates, the new value also has uncertainty. We should not simply add individual margins of error when adding estimates.

region <- county_data %>%
  filter(NAME %in% c(
    "Hamilton County, New York",
    "Essex County, New York",
    "Greene County, New York"
  ))

region_total <- sum(region$estimate)
region_total_moe <- moe_sum(region$moe, region$estimate)

region_total

[1] 9594

region_total_moe

[1] 889.1648


The tidycensus functions for derived uncertainty are:

moe_sum() for adding estimates
moe_prop() for one estimate as a share of another
moe_ratio() for a ratio where the numerator is not a subset of the denominator

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Proportions and moe_prop()
Suppose we want the proportion of people below poverty out of a total population. Both the numerator and denominator have estimates and margins of error.

poverty_share <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B07012_002",
    total = "B07012_001"
  ),
  state = "NY",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
) %>%
  mutate(
    share = below_povertyE / totalE,
    share_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE,
      totalE,
      below_povertyM,
      totalM
    ),
    share_pct = share * 100,
    share_moe_pct = share_moe * 100
  )

If the proportion is multiplied by 100, its margin of error must also be multiplied by 100.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Coefficient of Variation
The coefficient of variation, or CV, measures sampling error relative to the estimate:
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{Estimate} \times 100
\]
Because the ACS generally uses a 90% margin of error:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]
Therefore:
cv = (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100
A lower CV means less uncertainty relative to the estimate. A higher CV means more sampling uncertainty.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Change Over Time
ACS 5-year estimates cover overlapping periods:

The 2022 ACS 5-year estimate covers 2018–2022
The 2023 ACS 5-year estimate covers 2019–2023

For a cleaner comparison, use non-overlapping periods such as 2014–2018 and 2019–2023.
When comparing income across time, adjust for inflation before interpreting the difference.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Creating a Reusable Function
An R function is a reusable set of instructions. This function takes a year as an argument, downloads the data, and creates a period label.

get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = "B07012_002",
    state = "NY",
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr))
}

The function does not run when it is defined. It creates a recipe that can be used later.

poverty_change <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2018),
  get_poverty(2023)
)

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
section: Converting Long Data to Wide Data
text:
Converting Long Data to Wide Data
The repeated ACS results are initially in long format:



County
Period
Estimate




Albany County
2014–2018
10,000


Albany County
2019–2023
12,000



We can convert them to wide format so both periods appear in the same row:

poverty_wide <- poverty_change %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, estimate, moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(estimate, moe)
  )

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Calculating Change and Its Uncertainty

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change = `estimate_2019-2023` - `estimate_2014-2018`,
    se_1 = `moe_2014-2018` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `moe_2019-2023` / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

The difference between two estimates also has uncertainty. We calculate the standard error of the difference and use it to calculate a margin of error for the change.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Visualizing Significant Change

poverty_tested %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change), y = change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = change > 0)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = change - moe_diff, ymax = change + moe_diff),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistically Significant Change in Poverty Count",
    subtitle = "2014–2018 versus 2019–2023, ACS 5-year estimates",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in people below poverty level"
  )

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Creating a Reliability Table

reliability_table <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100,
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, estimate, moe, cv, flag)

reliability_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, moe), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "County",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    moe = "MOE",
    cv = "CV (%)",
    flag = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Reconstructing the comparison
I examine the broad claim that poverty increased in parts of Philadelphia in Alfred Lubrano’s December 6, 2018 article. I use B17001_002 (people below poverty) divided by B17001_001 (people for whom poverty status is determined). This measures poverty across all racial groups. I assume this table is an appropriate reconstruction because the article does not identify its exact variables or neighborhood-to-tract crosswalk. Tracts are not neighborhoods, so this analysis cannot reproduce the named neighborhood figures exactly.
The acs5 estimates ending in 2010 and 2017 cover 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. I use five-year estimates because they provide tract-level data and match the article’s neighborhood comparison. These periods do not overlap. I follow the class method of treating their sampling errors as independent when calculating uncertainty in the change.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B17001_002",
    total = "B17001_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)
head(poverty_2010) %>%
  select(-NAME) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(below_povertyE, below_povertyM, totalE, totalM), decimals = 0) %>%
  cols_label(GEOID = "Tract GEOID", below_povertyE = "Below poverty",
             below_povertyM = "Below poverty MOE", totalE = "Poverty universe",
             totalM = "Universe MOE") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Poverty count estimates: 2006–2010", subtitle = "First six Philadelphia tracts") %>%
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS B17001. Counts and 90% margins of error are in people.")

The poverty rate estimates need to be assessed for reliability before comparing the two periods. Using the CV thresholds from Jurjevich et al. (2018), estimates are classified as reliable below 12%, somewhat reliable from 12% to 40%, and unreliable above 40%.
CV measures uncertainty relative to the estimated rate. It is undefined when the rate is zero, even if the denominator is positive; that rate and its MOE can still be used to test change.


Show code

      cv < 12   ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40  ~ "Somewhat reliable",

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Interpreting change
A difference between the two poverty rates does not necessarily indicate a change beyond sampling uncertainty. The calculation below subtracts the earlier rate from the later rate and combines their uncertainty to produce a 90% confidence interval for the change.
If this interval excludes zero, the change is statistically significant. If it includes zero, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that poverty increased or decreased.
Here, zero means no change in the poverty rate, not a zero population denominator.
These are individual tract tests at 90% confidence, without an adjustment for multiple testing; they do not guarantee that every flagged change is real.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change = poverty_rate_2017 - poverty_rate_2010,

    se_2010 = poverty_moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2017 = poverty_moe_2017 / 1.645,

    se_diff = sqrt(se_2010^2 + se_2017^2),
    moe_diff = 1.645 * se_diff,

    lower = change - moe_diff,
    upper = change + moe_diff,

    z = change / na_if(se_diff, 0),
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

poverty_tested %>%
  select(GEOID, change, moe_diff, lower, upper, significant) %>%
  head() %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(change, moe_diff, lower, upper), decimals = 1) %>%
  sub_missing(missing_text = "Unavailable") %>%
  cols_label(GEOID = "Tract GEOID", change = "Change", moe_diff = "Change MOE",
             lower = "Lower bound", upper = "Upper bound", significant = "Significant?") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Testing poverty-rate changes", subtitle = "First six tracts: 2006–2010 to 2013–2017") %>%
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS B17001. Changes and 90% interval bounds are in percentage points. TRUE means significant at 90% confidence.")




Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_tested %>%
  mutate(
    change_result = case_when(
      is.na(significant)       ~ "Cannot assess",
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE                     ~ "No significant change"
    )
  )

poverty_tested %>%
  count(change_result) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(change_result = "Change classification", n = "Tracts") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Poverty-change results for all 384 tracts",
             subtitle = "Philadelphia: 2006–2010 to 2013–2017") %>%
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS B17001. Tests use 90% confidence; undefined changes are classified separately.")

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
section: Does the analysis support the article?
text:
Does the analysis support the article?
Supported: My results support the broad finding that poverty increased in some parts of Philadelphia. Comparing 2006–2010 with 2013–2017, I found statistically significant increases in 36 census tracts and decreases in 27, using a 90% confidence level. Another 313 tracts had no statistically significant change, and eight could not be assessed. Not supported: I cannot identify a specific neighborhood claim as contradicted or statistically unsupported without its tract aggregation and uncertainty estimates. Those claims remain in “Cannot be determined.” A result that is not statistically significant does not prove that poverty stayed the same.
Cannot be determined: I cannot determine whether Eastwick’s reported increase from 12% to 26% is statistically significant because the article does not identify the tracts used to construct its neighborhood figures. My analysis also measures poverty across all racial groups, so it cannot verify the claims about white poverty. I have not shown that a specific neighborhood’s numeric claim is false. The article acknowledges that ACS estimates have margins of error, but I would make that uncertainty more visible in the reporting. I would describe where change can be detected while keeping the neighborhood and race-specific claims separate from what this tract-level analysis establishes.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
section: How I would report the findings
text:
How I would report the findings
Poverty rates increased in some Philadelphia census tracts and decreased in others between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. An analysis of American Community Survey estimates found increases in 36 tracts and decreases in 27 that were statistically significant at the 90% confidence level. In 313 tracts, the estimates were too uncertain to establish a change; this does not mean poverty remained unchanged. Eight additional tracts could not be assessed because their poverty-rate denominators were zero in at least one period. These findings show an uneven pattern of detectable change, but they do not establish whether poverty rose citywide or confirm the article’s neighborhood and race-specific claims.
